steps.markdown: Run one test at the 0.05 level when nothing is going on, and you have a 5% chance of a false positive. Run many, and false positives pile up.
With 20 independent tests and no real effects, the chance of at least one "significant" result is 1 − 0.95²⁰ ≈ **0.64**, nearly two in three.
**p-hacking** is trying many analyses (subgroups, metrics, outlier rules) and reporting the one that worked. It produces findings that don't replicate.

Fixes: decide the metric and analysis *before* looking at data, correct for multiple tests (the **Bonferroni** correction divides 0.05 by the number of tests), and confirm surprising results on fresh data. The same logic applies when you try many models on one test set.
